## 

​

Settings files

The `settings.json` file is the official mechanism for configuring Claude Code through hierarchical settings:

  * User settings are defined in `~/.claude/settings.json` and apply to all projects.
  * Project settings are saved in your project directory:
    * `.claude/settings.json` for settings that are checked into source control and shared with your team
    * `.claude/settings.local.json` for settings that are not checked in, useful for personal preferences and experimentation. Claude Code will configure git to ignore `.claude/settings.local.json` when it is created.
  * Managed settings: For organizations that need centralized control, Claude Code supports multiple delivery mechanisms for managed settings. All use the same JSON format and cannot be overridden by user or project settings:
    * Server-managed settings: delivered from Anthropic’s servers via the Claude.ai admin console. Use these settings to reduce disk usage and startup time in large monorepos.

Key  | Description  | Example
--- | --- | ---
`worktree.symlinkDirectories`  | Directories to symlink from the main repository into each worktree to avoid duplicating large directories on disk. No directories are symlinked by default  | `["node_modules", ".cache"]`
`worktree.sparsePaths`  | Directories to check out in each worktree via git sparse-checkout (cone mode). Only the listed paths are written to disk, which is faster in large monorepos  | `["packages/my-app", "shared/utils"]`

To copy gitignored files like `.env` into new worktrees, use a `.worktreeinclude` file in your project root instead of a setting.

### 

​

Permission settings

Keys  | Description  | Example
--- | --- | ---
`allow`  | Array of permission rules to allow tool use. See Permission rule syntax below for pattern matching details  | `[ "Bash(git diff *)" ]`
`ask`  | Array of permission rules to ask for confirmation upon tool use.   2. Command line arguments
     * Temporary overrides for a specific session
  3. Local project settings (`.claude/settings.local.json`)
     * Personal project-specific settings
  4. Shared project settings (`.claude/settings.json`)
     * Team-shared project settings in source control
  5. User settings (`~/.claude/settings.json`)
     * Personal global settings
This hierarchy ensures that organizational policies are always enforced while still allowing teams and individuals to customize their experience. The same precedence applies whether you run Claude Code from the CLI, the VS Code extension, or a JetBrains IDE. For example, if your user settings allow `Bash(npm run *)` but a project’s shared settings deny it, the project setting takes precedence and the command is blocked.

Array settings merge across scopes. When the same array-valued setting (such as `sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` or `permissions.allow`) appears in multiple scopes, the arrays are concatenated and deduplicated, not replaced. This means lower-priority scopes can add entries without overriding those set by higher-priority scopes, and vice versa. For example, if managed settings set `allowWrite` to `["/opt/company-tools"]` and a user adds `["~/.kube"]`, both paths are included in the final configuration.

### 

​

Verify active settings

Run `/status` inside Claude Code to see which settings sources are active and where they come from. The output shows each configuration layer (managed, user, project) along with its origin, such as `Enterprise managed settings (remote)`, `Enterprise managed settings (plist)`, `Enterprise managed settings (HKLM)`, or `Enterprise managed settings (file)`. If a settings file contains errors, `/status` reports the issue so you can fix it.

Require marketplaces for your team

You can configure your repository so team members are automatically prompted to install your marketplace when they trust the project folder. Add your marketplace to `.claude/settings.json`:
    
    `{
      "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
        "company-tools": {
          "source": {
            "source": "github",
            "repo": "your-org/claude-plugins"
          }
        }
      }
    }

        "code-formatter@company-tools": true,
        "deployment-tools@company-tools": true
      }
    }

When you run Claude Code from a git worktree, the path still points at the main checkout, so all worktrees share the same marketplace location. L171: Subagents can run in their own worktrees so parallel edits don’t conflict. Ask Claude to “use worktrees for your agents”, or make the isolation permanent for a cite69†custom subagent by adding `isolation: worktree` to its frontmatter. This subagent in `.claude/agents/` always runs in its own worktree:
L172: 
L173:     `---
L174:     name: refactorer
L175:     description: Applies mechanical refactors across many files
L176:     isolation: worktree
L177:     ---
L178:     Apply the requested refactor across every affected file, then run the tests
L179:     and report the results.
L180:     `
L181: Each subagent gets a temporary worktree that Claude Code removes automatically when the subagent finishes without changes; a worktree with changes stays on disk until the cite41†periodic sweep below can remove it without losing work. Subagent worktrees use the same cite43†base branch as `--worktree`, so they branch from your repository’s default branch unless `worktree.baseRef` is set to `"head"`.
L182: ###
L183: 
L184: cite41†​ L185: 
L186: Clean up subagent and background-session worktrees
L187: 
L188: Claude Code runs a periodic sweep that removes worktrees that Claude created for subagents and cite67†background sessions once they are older than your cite70†`cleanupPeriodDays` setting, following the cite71†retention sweep rules . When you cite72†background a `--worktree` session, its worktree becomes a background-session worktree that the sweep can remove. The sweep leaves a worktree in place in these cases:
L189:   * The worktree still holds work: changed or untracked files, or unpushed commits.
L190:   * Claude Code can’t determine which filter drivers the repository config defines, in any of the cite54†three cases that also block worktree creation .
L191:   * The worktree belongs to a `--worktree` session you haven’t backgrounded, whatever its age.
L192:   * You created the worktree yourself with `git worktree add`, even if you then ran a `--worktree <name>` session in it and backgrounded that session.
L193: Claude Code writes a marker into the git metadata of every worktree it creates with git, and the sweep keeps any worktree without one, including a worktree a cite50†`WorktreeCreate` hook created. Before v2.1.246, the sweep didn’t check for the marker, and could remove a worktree you created yourself when an old background-session record pointed at it.
L194: While an agent is running, Claude Code holds a `git worktree lock` on its worktree so that concurrent cleanup can’t remove it, and releases the lock when the agent finishes. Claude Code holds the same lock on the worktree it created for a backgrounded session while the session runs, so the sweep leaves the worktree in place and `git worktree remove` refuses to remove it.
L195: The sweep also releases a lock Claude Code set for a session whose process has exited, so a killed background session doesn’t leave its worktree permanently locked. The sweep never releases a lock you set yourself with `git worktree lock`. Before v2.1.210, a lock left by a killed session stayed in place until you ran `git worktree unlock`. To clean up a worktree that the sweep keeps, run `git worktree remove`, adding `--force` if the worktree has uncommitted changes or untracked files.
L196: If git refuses because the worktree is locked, run `git worktree unlock` on it first.
L197: ##
L198: 
L199: cite42†​ L200: 
L201: Customize worktree creation
L202: 
L203: Claude Code’s defaults for creating worktrees cover most sessions: it creates them under `.claude/worktrees/`, branches them from your repository’s default branch, and checks out only tracked files. The options in this section change those defaults.
L204: ###
L205: 
L206: cite43†​ L207: 
L208: Choose the base branch
L209: 
L210: New worktrees branch from the repository’s default branch, so most sessions don’t need this setting. Set `worktree.baseRef` in cite73†settings to branch from your current work instead. The setting accepts two values:
L211:   * `"fresh"` (default): branch from the repository’s default branch on the remote, usually `main`, so the worktree starts from a clean tree matching the remote.
L212:   * `"head"`: branch from your current local `HEAD`, so the worktree carries your unpushed commits and feature-branch state. Use this when isolating subagents that need to operate on in-progress work. Inside a worktree, `"head"` resolves to that worktree’s `HEAD`, not the main checkout’s.
L213: You can’t set `worktree.baseRef` to a branch name. To start a worktree from a specific existing branch, cite49†create it with git directly . For a `"fresh"` base, Claude Code keeps `origin/HEAD` current: when the repository hasn’t been fetched in the last 24 hours, it fetches the default branch, capped at five seconds, and uses the locally cached ref if the fetch fails. If no remote is configured, or `origin/HEAD` isn’t cached locally and can’t be fetched, the worktree falls back to your current local `HEAD`.

L56: 
L57: Settings are the JSON keys that change how Claude Code behaves: which model it starts with, what it can run without asking, which files it can’t read, how it looks in your terminal, and what your organization enforces.
L58: To look up a specific key, go to cite40†All settings , which lists every key with the file you set it in, its default, and an example.
L59: Claude Code reads settings from JSON settings files such as `~/.claude/settings.json`. It looks for them in a few locations, and cite10†the file it reads a setting from decides who the setting applies to . This page covers those files: which one to put a setting in, how to change a setting and confirm it applied, and which value Claude Code uses when the same key is set in more than one file.
L60: cite41†Configure permissions covers what Claude Code can run without asking and how to write `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` rules.
L61: This page covers Claude Code running on your machine: the terminal, the cite42†VS Code and cite43†JetBrains extensions, and the cite44†desktop app , which all read the same settings files. L67: 
L68: Claude Code reads settings from four files, and an organization can also deliver managed settings from the claude.ai console. Each source has a scope: the set of people and projects a setting saved in it applies to, whether that’s just you, everyone in a project, or everyone in your organization.
L69: Scope  | File  | Who it affects  | Use it for
L70: --- | --- | --- | ---
L71: User  | `~/.claude/settings.json`  | You, in every project on this machine  | Personal preferences: theme, editor mode, default model, your own permission rules
L72: Shared project  | `.claude/settings.json`  | Everyone working in the folder that contains it. In a git repository, commit it so teammates get it  | Team permissions, hooks, plugins, and the environment variables the project needs
L73: Project local  | `.claude/settings.local.json`  | You, in this one project only. Claude Code keeps it out of git when it creates the file; if you create it by hand, add it to `.gitignore` yourself  | Personal overrides for one project, and testing before you share
L74: Managed  | `managed-settings.json` and other cite46†managed sources | Everyone your organization deploys it to; nothing you set overrides it, apart from a few cite37†security-sensitive exceptions | Security policy and compliance requirements
L75: In the File column, `~/.claude` is the `.claude` folder in your home directory, and a bare `.claude` is the `.claude` folder inside your project.
L76: ###
L77: 
L78: cite11†​ L79: 
L80: Compare the scope of each settings file
L81: 
L82: Suppose you have three projects on your machine, `website/`, `api/`, and `acme-app/`, a teammate has their own clone of `acme-app/`, and you start a cite38†cloud session on `acme-app/`. The graphic below shows which of those folders a setting applies in when you start Claude Code from them. Click a settings file to see the folders it reaches.
L83:   * `~/.claude/settings.json`: every project on your machine, and nothing on your teammate’s or in the cloud session
L84:   * `acme-app/.claude/settings.json`: your `acme-app/`. It reaches your teammate’s clone and the cloud session only if you commit the file to version control; until you do, it’s a file on your disk like any other and nobody else has it
L85:   * `acme-app/.claude/settings.local.json`: your `acme-app/` only. Claude Code adds it to your global git excludes the first time it writes the file, so it stays out of your commits; if you create the file by hand, cite14†add it to `.gitignore` yourself L86:   * Managed settings, whether a `managed-settings.json` file, an MDM policy, or cite47†server-managed settings from the claude.ai console: every project on every machine your organization deploys it to, or that you sign in to with your organization account. Only server-managed settings reach the cloud session

The short answer: only sometimes, and the channels contradict each other.

  1. The spelling problem. There are two names for the same command — `entire search` (experimental, hidden in stable builds) and `entire checkpoint search` (canonical, always visible). An agent following one surface's advice gets contradicted by another.

Both goals noted — full stack is fair game, and the work is reinforcement: make the channels that already exist consistent, truthful, and stronger, rather than adding new ones.

That frames the load-bearing design question, because most of the contradictions trace back to one decision:

What's the canonical spelling for search (and `why`)? The options:

  * A. Standardize on `entire checkpoint search` everywhere. It's already the canonical, always-visible path. Fix: search skill templates teach `checkpoint search --json --compact`, injection stays as-is, `agent-help checkpoint` remains the drill-down. For `why`: either promote it out of experimental or annotate it with `entire_agent_help` (the annotation `trail` uses) so `agent-help why` works in stable builds even while hidden.
  * B. Promote top-level `entire search` (and `why`) out of experimental. They become first-class visible commands in stable builds; injection, skill, labs, and agent-help all agree on the short spelling. More surface commitment — you're declaring the API stable.
  * C. Keep both spellings but make every advisory surface agree on one (the skill switches to whichever the injection names) and make `agent-help` resolve the other one instead of erroring.

Make `entire search` the canonical spelling: - Register it as a visible top-level command (Sessions & Checkpoints group) instead of behind the experimental gate; `checkpoint search` stays a working alias. - Point the first-turn context injection at `entire search`. - Fix the search skill templates' stale claim that explain is "current repo only" — `entire checkpoint explain <id> --repo <owner/name>` handles cross-repo hits (needs the full checkpoint ID); teach the same drill-down in the search command's help text. content.text: Claude’s documentation exposes a likely scope change in the second follow-up: since Claude Code 2.1.211, a linked worktree uses the main checkout’s `.claude/settings.local.json`. Shared `.claude/settings.json` still comes from the worktree checkout. That means the original failure remains possible for older Claude versions or missing shared files, but current Claude may already inherit local Entire hooks. I’m checking whether Entire’s present `status`/`doctor` logic already covers that case.

item.stdout:
---
name: review
description: Review a checked-out GitHub PR, local branch, or final landing diff; run optional second-model autoreview closeout; write paste-ready GitHub review comments. Use when the user asks to review a PR, review changed code, run autoreview/second-model review, do a landing review before push/merge/PR, or write Smit-style review wording.
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# Review

Review code that is already checked out locally. Read source from the worktree; use `gh` only for
metadata and comments. Never fetch file contents through `gh`.

## Pick Mode

- **PR review:** use when inside a `pr-<number>` worktree, or the user says `review this PR` / `review PR #N`.
- **Landing review:** use when the user wants a final blocker check before push, merge, or PR creation.
- **Autoreview closeout:** use when the user asks for Codex/Claude/autoreview/second-model review, or after non-trivial edits before commit/ship.
- **Review wording:** use when the user wants a paste-ready GitHub comment or Smit-style review summary.

## Do

1. **Scope the diff** against the merge base, don't guess:
   `git diff --stat $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` then the full diff, plus
   `git log --oneline $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD`. When the Entire Graph plugin is
   installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), add the entity-level view —
   `entire graph diff --base $(git merge-base main HEAD) --head HEAD --json` names the changed
   functions and types, and `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text` checks a
   changed symbol's callers before judging its contract.
2. **For PR review, determine the PR number** from the branch (`git branch --show-current`, e.g. `pr-49207`).
   If the branch is not `pr-<number>`, ask or use `gh pr view` metadata.
3. **For PR review, read prior reviews first.** Fetch human and bot reviews (Copilot, CodeRabbit,
   `github-actions[bot]`). Note what is flagged, resolved, or ongoing. Commands: see
   `references/gh-commands.md`.
4. **Read code locally** (Read/Grep/Glob), full modified files, not just diff hunks. Never
   `gh api` for file contents.
5. **Check for real risks:** correctness, edge/error handling, codebase consistency, missing tests/docs,
   panic-prone code, secrets, destructive operations, injection risk, auth gaps, data loss, swallowed
   errors, debug artifacts, and source comments that contain process metadata.
6. **Route boundary-sensitive changes through the focused lenses.** Apply `correctness-review` when
   the diff touches persistence, lifecycle, hooks, locking, subprocesses, path ownership, or external
   tool state. Also apply `blast-radius` when it changes a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess,
   or environment helper. Fold their evidence-backed findings into this review rather than listing
   the same issue twice.
7. **Check extensibility:** flag hard-coded runtime, provider, language, model, or prompt assumptions
   unless the PR explicitly targets only that path. Prefer configuration, registries, adapters, or
   prompt templates when the system should stay open to more variants.
8. **Cross-reference prior feedback:** if a human or bot already raised a finding, note agreement or
   disagreement rather than re-raising it.
9. **Use Smit voice only when requested:** read `references/smit-review-voice.md` and output plain
   paste-ready comment text rather than the working-notes template.
10. **Present the summary**, then ask whether to submit via `gh` or keep as notes. Don't submit
   unprompted.

## Autoreview Closeout

Use the bundled structured review helper as an advisory second-model pass. Codex is the default engine
when none is set. Full helper details live in `references/autoreview-helper.md`.

```bash
<autoreview-helper> --mode local                          # dirty local patch only
<autoreview-helper> --mode branch --base origin/main      # branch/PR work
<autoreview-helper> --mode commit --commit HEAD           # already-committed/landed work
```

---
name: using-entire
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
description: >
  Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical
  intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire
  skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
---

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

Also check whether the Entire Graph plugin is installed:

```bash
entire graph version
```

If it prints a version, the graph is available and **every code-locating step
in this skill must go through it** — never grep, find, or read whole files to
locate code when the graph can answer. The division of labor:

- **Structure** (where is X, what calls X, what breaks if X changes) → `entire graph`
- **Intent** (why is X like this, what was the developer thinking) → checkpoints

Graph command palette:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --format agent --top-k 5 \
  --query "<task in one sentence>"                                            # locate
entire graph def <symbol>                                                     # one definition
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in --format agent  # callers
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text                         # blast radius
entire graph commit <ref>                                                     # entity-level change list
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json                                    # semantic changes between refs
```

One search, then act — answer from the search output when it already suffices,
and read only a focused line range around reported locations. Skip the graph
when the task already names one small exact file. The full measured doctrine
lives in the `lean-mode` skill.

Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle: read focused source around the
reported `file:line` before relying on it. If `entire graph version` fails, the
plugin is absent — fall back to standard search tools without it.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Locate or trace code structure | "where is X implemented" / "what calls X" / "what would changing X affect" / "find the code that does Y" | run `entire graph` directly (`search`, `def`, `neighbors`, `impact`) |
| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `entire-teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |
| Code review with intent context | "review these changes" / "review this branch" / "audit before merging" | `entire-review` |
| Hand off to another agent | "hand off this session" / "continue in another agent" / "pick up the codex session" | `session-handoff` |
| Convert session to skill | "turn this into a skill" / "make a skill from this session" | `session-to-skill` |
| Link session to other repos | "link session to other repos" / "attach session to the foo repo" | `session-crosslink` |
| General exploration | "understand this module" / "explore how auth works" / "help me understand the codebase" | _(self — see below)_ |

If the scenario clearly maps to a sub-skill, delegate entirely to that skill's
workflow. Do not duplicate their steps here.

## General Exploration Flow

When no specific sub-skill fits — e.g. the user asks to "understand this
module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

1. **Identify key files** in the target area with the graph when it is
   installed:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the module or behavior to understand>"
```

Then map the neighborhood of the top hits (`neighbors` for callers,
`impact` for blast radius) instead of reading whole files. Without the graph
plugin, identify entry points, main types, and core functions manually.

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

Look for `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers in the commit bodies:

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

3. **Read intent for covered commits** — extract the checkpoint ID from the
   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

If you only have a commit hash (not a checkpoint ID), use:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

4. **Synthesize**: combine the recorded intent (from checkpoints) with the
   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

5. **Report** your findings, clearly distinguishing:
   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

## AI Agent Usage Notes

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire checkpoint explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding — still graph-first when the
   plugin is installed (`entire graph search` to locate, `neighbors`/`impact`
   to trace call sites), reading focused source around the results; check git
   log for history.
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

## References

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly
  documentation index following the [llms.txt standard](https://llmstxt.org),
  designed to be consumed directly by LLMs and coding agents

# Review

Review code that is already checked out locally. Read source from the worktree; use `gh` only for
metadata and comments. Never fetch file contents through `gh`.

## Pick Mode

- **PR review:** use when inside a `pr-<number>` worktree, or the user says `review this PR` / `review PR #N`.
- **Landing review:** use when the user wants a final blocker check before push, merge, or PR creation.
- **Autoreview closeout:** use when the user asks for Codex/Claude/autoreview/second-model review, or after non-trivial edits before commit/ship.
- **Review wording:** use when the user wants a paste-ready GitHub comment or Smit-style review summary.

## Do

1. **Scope the diff** against the merge base, don't guess:
   `git diff --stat $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD` then the full diff, plus
   `git log --oneline $(git merge-base main HEAD)..HEAD`. When the Entire Graph plugin is
   installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), add the entity-level view —
   `entire graph diff --base $(git merge-base main HEAD) --head HEAD --json` names the changed
   functions and types, and `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text` checks a
   changed symbol's callers before judging its contract.
2. **For PR review, determine the PR number** from the branch (`git branch --show-current`, e.g. `pr-49207`).
   If the branch is not `pr-<number>`, ask or use `gh pr view` metadata.
3. **For PR review, read prior reviews first.** Fetch human and bot reviews (Copilot, CodeRabbit,
   `github-actions[bot]`). Note what is flagged, resolved, or ongoing. Commands: see
   `references/gh-commands.md`.
4. **Read code locally** (Read/Grep/Glob), full modified files, not just diff hunks. Never
   `gh api` for file contents.
5. **Check for real risks:** correctness, edge/error handling, codebase consistency, missing tests/docs,
   panic-prone code, secrets, destructive operations, injection risk, auth gaps, data loss, swallowed
   errors, debug artifacts, and source comments that contain process metadata.
6. **Route boundary-sensitive changes through the focused lenses.** Apply `correctness-review` when
   the diff touches persistence, lifecycle, hooks, locking, subprocesses, path ownership, or external
   tool state. Also apply `blast-radius` when it changes a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess,
   or environment helper. Fold their evidence-backed findings into this review rather than listing
   the same issue twice.
7. **Check extensibility:** flag hard-coded runtime, provider, language, model, or prompt assumptions
   unless the PR explicitly targets only that path. Prefer configuration, registries, adapters, or
   prompt templates when the system should stay open to more variants.
8. **Cross-reference prior feedback:** if a human or bot already raised a finding, note agreement or
   disagreement rather than re-raising it.
9. **Use Smit voice only when requested:** read `references/smit-review-voice.md` and output plain
   paste-ready comment text rather than the working-notes template.
10. **Present the summary**, then ask whether to submit via `gh` or keep as notes. Don't submit
   unprompted.

## Autoreview Closeout

Use the bundled structured review helper as an advisory second-model pass. Codex is the default engine
when none is set. Full helper details live in `references/autoreview-helper.md`.

```bash
<autoreview-helper> --mode local                          # dirty local patch only
<autoreview-helper> --mode branch --base origin/main      # branch/PR work
<autoreview-helper> --mode commit --commit HEAD           # already-committed/landed work
```

- Verify every accepted finding by reading the real code path before fixing it.
- Reject noise: unrealistic edge cases, speculative risks, broad rewrites, and unrelated refactors.
- If a fix changes code, rerun focused tests and rerun the helper until no accepted/actionable findings remain.
- Be patient. A run can take up to 30 minutes while the model is active.
- Do not push just to review. Push only on explicit request.

## Output

For working notes, use this template:

```text
## PR #<number>: <title>
### Summary        <1-2 sentences on what it does>
### Changes        <brief file-by-file or logical grouping>
### Prior Reviews  <who flagged what, and whether addressed; "No prior reviews." if none>
### Feedback       <numbered NEW findings with file:line; mark agree/build-on vs. new>
### Verdict        <approve | request changes | comment>
```

For landing review, use this template:

```text
Landing review
- Critical blockers:
- Non-blocking follow-ups:
- Tests or checks still worth running:
```

For autoreview closeout, include the command used, tests/proof run, findings accepted/rejected with
brief why, and the clean result from the final helper run.

Stop after presenting. Use local tools for all code/diffing; use `gh` only for PR title/body,
labels, linked issues, comments, and `gh pr checks <number>`.
"}

Use when the user asks for a correctness review, asks whether a change is actually correct or safe to land, or is about to request review on work touching lifecycle, persistence, path resolution, locking, or an external tool's files.
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false

# Correctness Review

**A change is correct when you can name who owns the write, what happens if the process stops on
either side of it, and which test fails on the old code through the real seam.** A diff that reads
well and passes CI has cleared neither bar.

Distilled from the August 2026 Entire CLI review corpus -- nine authored PRs, 40 initial human
inline findings across 244 reviewed PRs. Almost none of the expensive findings were syntax. They
were ownership, state classification, duplicated policy, and tests that watched a nearby
abstraction instead of the failure.

## Use When

- Before requesting review on your own change, or reviewing someone else's diff for correctness
  rather than style.
- The change touches lifecycle, sessions, checkpoints, persistence, hooks, auth, path resolution,
  locking, subprocesses, or files another tool owns.
- Not for abstraction quality and file growth -- that is `thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`.
  Not for cost -- that is `perf-review`. Not for what breaks outside the diff -- that is
  `blast-radius`. This lens is about whether the change is *true*.

## The three questions

1. **Who owns the write?**
2. **What happens if the process stops immediately before or after the write?**
3. **Which test observes the real contract breaking on the old code?**

If any answer is vague, the change is not ready for review. Answer these first. Everything below
is how to get crisp answers.

## Do

1. **Map the state machine before judging a transition.** For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth,
   or layout work, write the one-page model first: read owner, write owner, migration owner,
   recovery owner; durable state versus temporary state; the operation that makes it irreversible;
   the retry owner after each interruption point; the caller's time budget and every blocking call
   inside it; the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure. Patching one
   transition without the table is the single most expensive mistake in the corpus.

2. **Trace failures to the outermost outcome.** Follow each new error, timeout, cancellation, and
   skipped operation through every caller to the command, hook, request, or job that the user
   observes. When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds),
   enumerate that caller chain with `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`
   (direct + transitive callers in one call) and verify against source — the graph can miss
   dynamic dispatch, so it bounds the trace rather than settling it. A safe helper can still be wrong when its error aborts an unrelated workflow. Do not
   approve an internal error policy until you can name the terminal exit status and user-visible
   result it produces.

3. **Audit interruption while resources are held.** For every state that owns a lock, transaction,
   pipe, temporary file, goroutine, or child process, cancel there and identify the cleanup path.
   Process exit is not proof that the domain operation succeeded. After failure, perform the next
   real operation that would expose leaked state; an error assertion alone does not prove cleanup.

4. **Separate safety, liveness, and fairness.** Prove independently that the change cannot corrupt
   state, can eventually make progress, and does not let one caller repeatedly jump queued callers.
   When a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess, or environment helper changes, compare callers
   with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline, and neither. A local fix that changes shared
   blocking or scheduling semantics has a wider contract than its motivating caller.

5. **Separate discovery from mutation authority.** Answer these apart, out loud: which file does
   the external tool read; which file may this command *inspect*; which file may this command
   *mutate*; who owns migration between them; what the user sees when those answers differ.
   Finding a path never grants permission to write to it.

6. **Classify states positively.** `absent` means the OS returned not-exist -- nothing else does.
   `unreadable`, `invalid`, `outdated`, `unresolved`, and `unsupported` are separate states with
   separate remedies. Unknown is not absent. Skipped is not success.

7. **Find the one owner of each decision.** If two functions answer the same eligibility question,
   make them call one predicate. Short duplicated policy is more dangerous than long duplicated
   formatting: one condition drifts and ownership or recovery silently changes. Search by
   responsibility and invariant, not by the symbol name you were about to add.

8. **Push the fix to the deepest boundary that can enforce the invariant once for all callers.**
   Normalize where data becomes permanent rather than pretending the current writer is the only
   producer. Preserve the wire format while you do it.

9. **Prove the test is real.** It fails on the old code for the reported reason, enters through the
   production seam that owns the behavior, and asserts the durable artifact or external result --
   not an intermediate value. Add a negative control. Cover every backend that owns the same
   contract. Use the real `git`, the real protocol, the real lock when that is the source of truth.

10. **Trace every claim to the branch that makes it true.** Comments, status text, warnings,
   remedies, and the PR body are part of the contract. If a message says "removed", a mutation
   happened. If a remedy says "run X", X can fix this exact state. Name the actual recovery owner.

11. **Walk the edge-case matrix** in `references/edge-case-matrix.md` for the categories the change
   touches. These are ordinary Git, filesystem, process, and terminal states, not exotic ones.

12. **Treat every automated finding as a hypothesis.** Reproduce it, check the module's language and
   tool versions, and reply with the mechanism. Do not change correct code to satisfy a linter bot
   working from an outdated model of the language.

13. **Re-scope the moment review changes the ownership model.** Stop patching the old shape. Split
    discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration into separate changes whose
    ownership decisions can be reviewed independently.

## Findings

`references/failure-patterns.md` has the seven recurring shapes with worked examples. Scan for them
by name; each one is a finding when present:

- a transition patched without its state machine;
- write ownership inferred from path proximity;
- an error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success;
- the same decision ladder in two places;
- a test on a nearby abstraction instead of the production failure;
- output, a comment, or a PR claim the code does not guarantee;
- one diff carrying discovery, mutation, migration, and diagnostics before the contract settled.

## Output

- **The system model**, in a few lines: read owner, write owner, durable write, interruption
  behavior, recovery owner, and outermost user-visible outcome. Say plainly when the change does
  not touch one.
- **Findings**, each with a `file:line`, the pattern it matches, and the state or interruption that
  makes it wrong -- concrete inputs to a wrong result, not a category name.
- **The three questions, answered.** Vague answers are themselves the top finding.
- **Cleanup proof.** Name the real operation performed after failure to prove no residual state
  survives, or mark that property unproven.
- **Cleared.** Which matrix rows you checked and found handled.

---
name: entire-review
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
description: >
  Review code changes on the current branch using checkpoint transcript context
  to understand developer intent before auditing the diff. Use when the user
  asks for a code review, wants to review branch changes, or asks to audit
  recent work before merging.
---

# Review

Review code changes on the current branch by first reading checkpoint transcripts to
understand the intent behind each change, then auditing the actual diff for issues.
This produces an intent-aware review that catches mismatches between what the developer
wanted and what the code actually does.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Review:`

followed by a blank line, then the content.

- Apply the header to the **first response of the invocation only.** Do not re-print it on
  follow-up turns within the same invocation.
- Do **not** include the header on error or early-exit responses (e.g. "not a git repository",
  "no commits found between branch and base").

## Rules

1. This is a **read-only audit**. Do not modify any files during the review.
2. Always show a scope banner before findings so the user knows what is being reviewed.
3. If checkpoint context is unavailable, still perform the review using only the diff and
   commit messages. Clearly state that the review lacks intent context.
4. Group findings by file. Within each file, order by severity (Critical > High > Medium > Low).
5. Every finding must include a concrete suggestion or explanation, not just flag the issue.
6. After presenting findings, ask the user if they want a fix plan. Do not auto-fix.
7. Do not review generated files, lock files, or binary files unless the user explicitly
   asks for them.

## Process

### 1. Verify environment

Run `entire version` to check if the CLI is available. If it is not installed, note that
the review will proceed without checkpoint intent context (degraded mode).

### 2. Detect base ref

Find the mainline branch to diff against. Try these refs in order and use the first that
exists:

```bash
git rev-parse --verify origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify origin/main 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify origin/master 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify main 2>/dev/null
git rev-parse --verify master 2>/dev/null
```

If none exist, tell the user no base ref was found and ask them to specify one.

### 3. Compute scope

```bash
git rev-list --count <base>..HEAD
git diff --stat <base>..HEAD
```

Record the number of commits and files changed. This forms the scope banner.

### 4. Gather checkpoint intent (skip in degraded mode)

```bash
git log --format='%H%x00%s%x00%b' <base>..HEAD
```

Extract `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer values from commit bodies. Deduplicate checkpoint IDs.

For each unique checkpoint ID (up to 20):

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

Parse the JSON to extract session metadata. For each non-review session in the checkpoint,
prefer the summary (intent + outcome). If no summary is available, fall back to the latest
user prompt. Truncate each checkpoint detail to 320 characters.

If `--json` fails for a checkpoint, fall back to the bare human-readable output:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --no-pager
```

Do not use `--full` in the review workflow — it produces long narrative text harder for
agents to parse in bulk. If that also fails, skip the checkpoint and note it was unavailable.

Additionally, read the current in-progress session (if any) for uncommitted work context:

```bash
entire session current --json
```

If this returns valid JSON, extract `last_prompt` and `files_touched` — these represent
the intent behind uncommitted changes that are not yet captured in any checkpoint.

Build an intent map: for each file in the diff (committed + uncommitted), collect the
relevant intent context from all checkpoints and the active session that touched it.

### 5. Read the diff

When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds), get the
entity-level change list first — it names exactly which functions and types changed,
which orders the file-by-file review and pairs each change with its checkpoint intent:

```bash
entire graph diff --base <base> --head HEAD --json
```

For any changed symbol whose contract matters, check callers before judging it:
`entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`. Skip both silently when the
plugin is absent.

```bash
git diff <base>..HEAD
```

Also include uncommitted changes:

```bash
git diff HEAD
```

For large diffs (>5000 lines total), focus on the most critical files:
- Files with the most changes
- Files mentioned in checkpoint intents
- Source files over generated/config files

Read individual file diffs as needed rather than loading the entire diff at once.

### 6. Perform the review

Read the review rules:

```
references/review-rules.md
```

For each file in the diff, review it considering:

**With checkpoint context:**
- Does the implementation match the stated intent?
- Were the constraints from the transcript respected?
- Did the agent miss edge cases it discussed?
- Are there leftover debugging artifacts or TODOs?

**Always (with or without context):**
- Logic errors, off-by-one, null safety
- Security issues (injection, auth bypass, data exposure)
- Performance concerns (N+1 queries, unnecessary allocations)
- Error handling gaps
- API contract violations

name: correctness-review
description: Correctness pass over a change -- who owns the write, what survives an interruption, whether the test observes the real contract, and whether the output claims more than the code proves. Use when the user asks for a correctness review, asks whether a change is actually correct or safe to land, or is about to request review on work touching lifecycle, persistence, path resolution, locking, or an external tool's files.
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
---

# Correctness Review

**A change is correct when you can name who owns the write, what happens if the process stops on
either side of it, and which test fails on the old code through the real seam.** A diff that reads
well and passes CI has cleared neither bar.

Distilled from the August 2026 Entire CLI review corpus -- nine authored PRs, 40 initial human
inline findings across 244 reviewed PRs. Almost none of the expensive findings were syntax. They
were ownership, state classification, duplicated policy, and tests that watched a nearby
abstraction instead of the failure.

## Use When

- Before requesting review on your own change, or reviewing someone else's diff for correctness
  rather than style.
- The change touches lifecycle, sessions, checkpoints, persistence, hooks, auth, path resolution,
  locking, subprocesses, or files another tool owns.
- Not for abstraction quality and file growth -- that is `thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review`.
  Not for cost -- that is `perf-review`. Not for what breaks outside the diff -- that is
  `blast-radius`. This lens is about whether the change is *true*.

## The three questions

1. **Who owns the write?**
2. **What happens if the process stops immediately before or after the write?**
3. **Which test observes the real contract breaking on the old code?**

If any answer is vague, the change is not ready for review. Answer these first. Everything below
is how to get crisp answers.

## Do

1. **Map the state machine before judging a transition.** For lifecycle, checkpoint, hook, auth,
   or layout work, write the one-page model first: read owner, write owner, migration owner,
   recovery owner; durable state versus temporary state; the operation that makes it irreversible;
   the retry owner after each interruption point; the caller's time budget and every blocking call
   inside it; the user-visible state for success, partial success, and failure. Patching one
   transition without the table is the single most expensive mistake in the corpus.

2. **Trace failures to the outermost outcome.** Follow each new error, timeout, cancellation, and
   skipped operation through every caller to the command, hook, request, or job that the user
   observes. When the Entire Graph plugin is installed (`entire graph version` succeeds),
   enumerate that caller chain with `entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text`
   (direct + transitive callers in one call) and verify against source — the graph can miss
   dynamic dispatch, so it bounds the trace rather than settling it. A safe helper can still be wrong when its error aborts an unrelated workflow. Do not
   approve an internal error policy until you can name the terminal exit status and user-visible
   result it produces.

3. **Audit interruption while resources are held.** For every state that owns a lock, transaction,
   pipe, temporary file, goroutine, or child process, cancel there and identify the cleanup path.
   Process exit is not proof that the domain operation succeeded. After failure, perform the next
   real operation that would expose leaked state; an error assertion alone does not prove cleanup.

4. **Separate safety, liveness, and fairness.** Prove independently that the change cannot corrupt
   state, can eventually make progress, and does not let one caller repeatedly jump queued callers.
   When a shared lock, retry, context, subprocess, or environment helper changes, compare callers
   with a deadline, cancellation without a deadline, and neither. A local fix that changes shared
   blocking or scheduling semantics has a wider contract than its motivating caller.

5. **Separate discovery from mutation authority.** Answer these apart, out loud: which file does
   the external tool read; which file may this command *inspect*; which file may this command
   *mutate*; who owns migration between them; what the user sees when those answers differ.
   Finding a path never grants permission to write to it.

6. **Classify states positively.** `absent` means the OS returned not-exist -- nothing else does.
   `unreadable`, `invalid`, `outdated`, `unresolved`, and `unsupported` are separate states with
   separate remedies. Unknown is not absent. Skipped is not success.

7. **Find the one owner of each decision.** If two functions answer the same eligibility question,
   make them call one predicate. Short duplicated policy is more dangerous than long duplicated
   formatting: one condition drifts and ownership or recovery silently changes. Search by
   responsibility and invariant, not by the symbol name you were about to add.

8. **Push the fix to the deepest boundary that can enforce the invariant once for all callers.**
   Normalize where data becomes permanent rather than pretending the current writer is the only
   producer. Preserve the wire format while you do it.

9. **Prove the test is real.** It fails on the old code for the reported reason, enters through the
   production seam that owns the behavior, and asserts the durable artifact or external result --
   not an intermediate value. Add a negative control. Cover every backend that owns the same
   contract. Use the real `git`, the real protocol, the real lock when that is the source of truth.

10. **Trace every claim to the branch that makes it true.** Comments, status text, warnings,
   remedies, and the PR body are part of the contract. If a message says "removed", a mutation
   happened. If a remedy says "run X", X can fix this exact state. Name the actual recovery owner.

11. **Walk the edge-case matrix** in `references/edge-case-matrix.md` for the categories the change
   touches. These are ordinary Git, filesystem, process, and terminal states, not exotic ones.

12. **Treat every automated finding as a hypothesis.** Reproduce it, check the module's language and
   tool versions, and reply with the mechanism. Do not change correct code to satisfy a linter bot
   working from an outdated model of the language.

13. **Re-scope the moment review changes the ownership model.** Stop patching the old shape. Split
    discovery, mutation, migration, diagnostics, and integration into separate changes whose
    ownership decisions can be reviewed independently.

## Findings

`references/failure-patterns.md` has the seven recurring shapes with worked examples. Scan for them
by name; each one is a finding when present:

- a transition patched without its state machine;
- write ownership inferred from path proximity;
- an error collapsed into absence, or a skip reported as success;
- the same decision ladder in two places;
- a test on a nearby abstraction instead of the production failure;
- output, a comment, or a PR claim the code does not guarantee;
- one diff carrying discovery, mutation, migration, and diagnostics before the contract settled.

## Output

- **The system model**, in a few lines: read owner, write owner, durable write, interruption
  behavior, recovery owner, and outermost user-visible outcome. Say plainly when the change does
  not touch one.
- **Findings**, each with a `file:line`, the pattern it matches, and the state or interruption that
  makes it wrong -- concrete inputs to a wrong result, not a category name.
- **The three questions, answered.** Vague answers are themselves the top finding.
- **Cleanup proof.** Name the real operation performed after failure to prove no residual state
  survives, or mark that property unproven.
- **Cleared.** Which matrix rows you checked and found handled.
"}

# Review Rules

This file defines the severity levels, audit dimensions, and output format for the
`review` skill. The SKILL.md workflow reads this file at review time.

## Severity Levels

Every finding must begin with one of these severity prefixes. These prefixes are parsed
by `entire review --fix` to extract individual findings for automated remediation.

| Severity | Prefix | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Critical | `Critical:` | Likely bug, data loss, or security vulnerability that must be fixed before merge | Null dereference, SQL injection, race condition, auth bypass, unvalidated redirect, use-after-free |
| High | `High:` | Serious issue that strongly warrants fixing | Missing error handling on I/O, N+1 queries in hot path, resource leak (fd/connection/goroutine), unsafe deserialization, hardcoded secret |
| Medium | `Medium:` | Improvement that reduces risk or improves maintainability | Unclear naming, duplicated logic, missing type constraints, excessive coupling, missing input validation on internal API |
| Low | `Low:` | Observation worth noting but not blocking | Style inconsistency, potential future tech debt, optional micro-optimization, missing logging |

## Audit Dimensions

### With checkpoint context (intent-aware review)

When checkpoint transcripts are available for a file, also check:

- **Intent match** — Does the implementation do what the user/agent described in the session?
- **Constraint adherence** — Were explicitly discussed constraints (performance, backward
  compatibility, API contracts) respected in the final code?
- **Edge case coverage** — Were edge cases mentioned in the transcript actually handled?
- **Leftover artifacts** — Are there debugging `console.log`, `TODO`/`FIXME` comments,
  commented-out code, or temporary workarounds that should have been cleaned up?
- **Scope creep** — Did the change introduce unrelated modifications not discussed in the
  session that could have side effects?

### Always check (with or without context)

These checks apply to every file in the diff regardless of checkpoint availability:

- **Logic errors** — Off-by-one, incorrect boolean logic, wrong comparison operator,
  infinite loops, unreachable branches, incorrect short-circuit evaluation
- **Null safety** — Unguarded nullable access, missing nil/undefined checks before
  dereference, optional chaining gaps
- **Security** — SQL/NoSQL injection, command injection, path traversal, XSS, CSRF,
  auth bypass, insecure direct object reference, data exposure in logs/errors,
  hardcoded credentials or secrets
- **Performance** — N+1 queries, unnecessary allocations in loops, missing pagination,
  unbounded collection growth, synchronous I/O in async context, missing indexes
- **Error handling** — Swallowed errors, missing catch/recover, error messages that leak
  internals, panic in library code, missing cleanup on error path
- **API contracts** — Return type mismatches, missing required fields, breaking changes
  to public interfaces, incorrect HTTP status codes, missing content-type headers
- **Concurrency** — Unprotected shared state, missing locks, goroutine/promise leaks,
  deadlock potential, race conditions on read-modify-write
- **Resource management** — Unclosed handles (files, connections, streams), missing
  `defer`/`finally`/`using`, leaked timers or intervals
- **Dead code** — Unreachable branches after early returns, unused imports/variables/functions,
  redundant conditions that are always true/false
- **Test quality** — Tests that never fail, assertions on implementation details rather
  than behavior, missing edge case coverage for new code paths

## Output Format

### With checkpoint context

```
Critical: <short issue description>
  Intent: <what the checkpoint said this should do>
  Actual: <what the code actually does>
  Fix: <concrete, actionable suggestion>
```

### Without checkpoint context

```
High: <short issue description>
  Issue: <what is wrong and why it matters>
  Fix: <concrete, actionable suggestion>
```

### Guidelines

- Keep the issue description on the severity line concise (one sentence).
- The `Intent:` line should quote or paraphrase the checkpoint transcript, not invent intent.
- The `Fix:` line must be specific enough to act on — name the function, variable, or
  pattern to change. Do not say "fix the bug" or "handle the error."
- When multiple findings affect the same logical issue (e.g., the same missing null check
  in three call sites), group them as one finding and list all affected locations.
- Do not flag style preferences unless they violate project-level conventions visible in
  the diff (e.g., an established linter config or formatter output).

# Edge-case matrix

Walk the categories the change touches. These are ordinary states, not exotic ones -- every row
below appeared as a real review finding or a real bug.

## Git and paths

- [ ] Normal checkout
- [ ] Conventional linked worktree
- [ ] `.bare/worktrees` layout
- [ ] Separate Git directory
- [ ] Ordinary submodule
- [ ] Linked submodule
- [ ] Symlinked checkout or directory
- [ ] Symlinked final file, and dangling symlink
- [ ] Missing, unreadable, malformed, and non-regular paths
- [ ] Path containment still holds *after* symlink resolution
- [ ] No remote, fork remote, raw URL, multiple push URLs, elected remote

## State and persistence

- [ ] Absent
- [ ] User-owned but not managed by this tool
- [ ] Partial
- [ ] Current
- [ ] Outdated
- [ ] Invalid
- [ ] Unreadable
- [ ] Unresolved
- [ ] Unsupported
- [ ] Older persisted format
- [ ] Unknown fields preserved on rewrite
- [ ] Nil versus empty serialized values (`null` versus `[]`)

## Process and concurrency

- [ ] Cancellation before the durable write
- [ ] Cancellation during each state that holds an external resource or prepared transaction
- [ ] Cancellation after the write but before state save
- [ ] Graceful abort releases locks, temporary files, pipes, goroutines, and child processes
- [ ] The next real operation succeeds immediately after cancellation or failure
- [ ] Lock contention and lock timeout
- [ ] Safety, liveness, and fairness evaluated separately
- [ ] Deadline-bearing, cancelable-without-deadline, and non-cancelable callers retain their contract
- [ ] Shared blocking, polling, or retry changes audited across all caller classes
- [ ] Concurrent writer from another process (the real one, not an in-process stand-in)
- [ ] Cleanup that removes state a later step needs
- [ ] Retry after a partial operation
- [ ] Idempotent rerun

## Environment and user interaction

- [ ] Variable unset
- [ ] Variable present but empty
- [ ] Tool-specific inherited variables cannot override the explicitly selected target
- [ ] Ambient variables poisoned in tests to prove repository, config, and credential isolation
- [ ] No TTY
- [ ] Raw-mode TTY
- [ ] `NO_COLOR` or non-styled output
- [ ] Windows and missing POSIX shell
- [ ] Expired, missing, and explicitly selected login contexts

## Failure semantics

- [ ] Typed sentinel errors matched with `errors.Is`, never by string
- [ ] Presence distinguished from a non-empty value (`os.LookupEnv`)
- [ ] Caller cancellation propagated separately from a child timeout
- [ ] Process exit success distinguished from domain-operation success
- [ ] Protocol response, process result, and local cancellation state agree
- [ ] Internal timeout or contention traced to the outermost command, hook, request, or job result
- [ ] Contention or temporary unavailability is not reported as a data conflict
- [ ] Context-aware lock acquisition wherever a context exists
- [ ] The underlying error preserved unless the public contract deliberately replaces it
- [ ] A silent-error type used only when the command already printed the user-facing error
- [ ] Unreadable, malformed, or unresolved never turned into absent
- [ ] No success reported after skipping every requested target

## User-visible contract

- [ ] Every status has a distinct meaning
- [ ] Every success message follows a confirmed success
- [ ] Every warning names the affected path, remote, context, or agent when that helps
- [ ] Every remedy can fix the exact state that printed it
- [ ] The command does not print the same error twice
- [ ] Comments and docs name the actual recovery owner and execution path

## Test hygiene

- [ ] Focused test shown failing on the old code, then passing
- [ ] Entry through the production seam, not a nearby helper
- [ ] Outermost affected workflow result asserted, not only the helper's return value
- [ ] Assertion on the durable artifact or external result
- [ ] Aftermath checked with the next real operation that would expose leaked state
- [ ] Negative control proving unrelated behavior did not change
- [ ] Every backend that owns the same contract covered
- [ ] Native tooling or the real protocol used where it is the source of truth
- [ ] Real lock held, or the real competing operation run, for concurrency claims
- [ ] Related log fields asserted on the same record
- [ ] Raw serialized bytes asserted when encoding shape is part of the contract
- [ ] Parallel by default, except where the test mutates process-global state
- [ ] Isolated temporary repository, config directory, cache, and token storage
- [ ] No spawned binary inherits an interactive terminal

## Language-level choices that encode semantics (Go)

- Keep `ctx` bound to the caller context; name a derived timeout for its purpose
  (`discoveryCtx`), never shadow the caller's.
- Distinguish `os.ErrNotExist` from permission and I/O errors.
- Keep atomic writes, containment validation, and symlink policy together -- atomic replacement
  alone does not define safe ownership.
- Preserve file modes and unknown fields when editing user-owned configuration.
- Create a happens-before edge with a channel, mutex, or atomic in race-tested code.
- Treat `exec.Cmd.Wait` as a process result, not proof that a child protocol committed its operation.
- Inspect `exec.Cmd.Cancel` before using the default kill behavior for a stateful child protocol.
- Record local cancellation state when a cooperative child abort can still exit successfully.
- Close resources at the right lifetime boundary; a cleanup that deletes state is not the same
  operation as terminating a process.
- Check the module's language version before accepting syntax advice.

{"chunk_id":"2de764","wall_time_seconds":0.000002541,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1188,"output":"# Review Rules

This file defines the severity levels, audit dimensions, and output format for the
`review` skill. The SKILL.md workflow reads this file at review time.

## Severity Levels

Every finding must begin with one of these severity prefixes. These prefixes are parsed
by `entire review --fix` to extract individual findings for automated remediation.

| Severity | Prefix | Meaning | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Critical | `Critical:` | Likely bug, data loss, or security vulnerability that must be fixed before merge | Null dereference, SQL injection, race condition, auth bypass, unvalidated redirect, use-after-free |
| High | `High:` | Serious issue that strongly warrants fixing | Missing error handling on I/O, N+1 queries in hot path, resource leak (fd/connection/goroutine), unsafe deserialization, hardcoded secret |
| Medium | `Medium:` | Improvement that reduces risk or improves maintainability | Unclear naming, duplicated logic, missing type constraints, excessive coupling, missing input validation on internal API |
| Low | `Low:` | Observation worth noting but not blocking | Style inconsistency, potential future tech debt, optional micro-optimization, missing logging |

## Audit Dimensions

### With checkpoint context (intent-aware review)

When checkpoint transcripts are available for a file, also check:

- **Intent match** — Does the implementation do what the user/agent described in the session?
- **Constraint adherence** — Were explicitly discussed constraints (performance, backward
  compatibility, API contracts) respected in the final code?
- **Edge case coverage** — Were edge cases mentioned in the transcript actually handled?
- **Leftover artifacts** — Are there debugging `console.log`, `TODO`/`FIXME` comments,
  commented-out code, or temporary workarounds that should have been cleaned up?
- **Scope creep** — Did the change introduce unrelated modifications not discussed in the
  session that could have side effects?

### Always check (with or without context)

These checks apply to every file in the diff regardless of checkpoint availability:

- **Logic errors** — Off-by-one, incorrect boolean logic, wrong comparison operator,
  infinite loops, unreachable branches, incorrect short-circuit evaluation
- **Null safety** — Unguarded nullable access, missing nil/undefined checks before
  dereference, optional chaining gaps
- **Security** — SQL/NoSQL injection, command injection, path traversal, XSS, CSRF,
  auth bypass, insecure direct object reference, data exposure in logs/errors,
  hardcoded credentials or secrets
- **Performance** — N+1 queries, unnecessary allocations in loops, missing pagination,
  unbounded collection growth, synchronous I/O in async context, missing indexes
- **Error handling** — Swallowed errors, missing catch/recover, error messages that leak
  internals, panic in library code, missing cleanup on error path
- **API contracts** — Return type mismatches, missing required fields, breaking changes
  to public interfaces, incorrect HTTP status codes, missing content-type headers
- **Concurrency** — Unprotected shared state, missing locks, goroutine/promise leaks,
  deadlock potential, race conditions on read-modify-write
- **Resource management** — Unclosed handles (files, connections, streams), missing
  `defer`/`finally`/`using`, leaked timers or intervals
- **Dead code** — Unreachable branches after early returns, unused imports/variables/functions,
  redundant conditions that are always true/false
- **Test quality** — Tests that never fail, assertions on implementation details rather
  than behavior, missing edge case coverage for new code paths

## Output Format

### With checkpoint context

```
Critical: <short issue description>
  Intent: <what the checkpoint said this should do>
  Actual: <what the code actually does>
  Fix: <concrete, actionable suggestion>
```

### Without checkpoint context

```
High: <short issue description>
  Issue: <what is wrong and why it matters>
  Fix: <concrete, actionable suggestion>
```

### Guidelines

- Keep the issue description on the severity line concise (one sentence).
- The `Intent:` line should quote or paraphrase the checkpoint transcript, not invent intent.
- The `Fix:` line must be specific enough to act on — name the function, variable, or
  pattern to change. Do not say "fix the bug" or "handle the error."
- When multiple findings affect the same logical issue (e.g., the same missing null check
  in three call sites), group them as one finding and list all affected locations.
- Do not flag style preferences unless they violate project-level conventions visible in
  the diff (e.g., an established linter config or formatter output).
"}

// Package gitexec runs the git CLI from inside the codebase. Callers that
// need plain stdout from `git <args>` (e.g. parsing `rev-parse HEAD`
// output) get a shared exec.Command + stderr-capture + error-wrap helper.
package gitexec

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
)

// Run runs `git <args>` in repoRoot and returns stdout as a string.
// stderr is captured separately and surfaced in the error wrap on non-zero
// exit. Stdout and stderr are NOT combined — git emits warnings on stderr
// even on successful commands (shallow-clone notices, safe.directory
// advisories, etc.) and merging them would corrupt parsed output (e.g.,
// strconv.Atoi on the result of `rev-list --count` would fail).
func Run(ctx context.Context, repoRoot string, args ...string) (string, error) {
	cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", args...)
	cmd.Dir = repoRoot
	var stderr strings.Builder
	cmd.Stderr = &stderr
	out, err := cmd.Output()
	if err != nil {
		stderrTxt := strings.TrimSpace(stderr.String())
		if stderrTxt != "" {
			return "", fmt.Errorf("git %s: %w (stderr: %s)", args[0], err, stderrTxt)
		}
		return "", fmt.Errorf("git %s: %w", args[0], err)
	}
	return string(out), nil
}

// HeadSHA returns the current HEAD commit hash as a 40-char hex string.
func HeadSHA(ctx context.Context, repoRoot string) (string, error) {
	out, err := Run(ctx, repoRoot, "rev-parse", "HEAD")
	if err != nil {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("git rev-parse HEAD: %w", err)
	}
	return strings.TrimSpace(out), nil
}
"}

entire enable — Enable Entire in current repository
Enable Entire with session tracking for your AI agent workflows.

If Entire is not yet configured, this runs the full configuration flow.
If Entire is already configured but disabled, this re-enables it.

If the current directory is not a git repository, Entire can initialize one
for you and (optionally) create a matching GitHub repository via the gh CLI.

Current repo: gh/MuskanPaliwal/cli  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

Flags:
      --absolute-git-hook-path               Embed full binary path in git hooks (for GUI git clients that don't source shell profiles)
      --agent string                         Agent to set up hooks for (e.g., claude-code, codex, copilot-cli, cursor, factoryai-droid, gemini, opencode, pi; external agents on $PATH are also available). Enables non-interactive mode.
      --agent-help-skill entire agent-help   Install the stable Entire agent-help skill (points agents at entire agent-help) for selected agent(s)
      --checkpoint-backend string            Checkpoint storage backend: refs (default; one git ref per checkpoint) or branch (legacy shared entire/checkpoints/v1 branch)
      --checkpoint-remote string             Checkpoint remote in provider:owner/repo format (e.g., github:org/checkpoints-repo)
  -f, --force                                Force reinstall hooks (removes existing Entire hooks first)
      --import-history                       During first-time setup, import the selected agents' existing session history (last 30 days) without prompting
      --init-repo                            If not a git repo, initialize one non-interactively
      --initial-commit-message string        Commit message for the initial commit when bootstrapping a new repo
      --local                                Write settings to .entire/settings.local.json instead of .entire/settings.json
      --no-github                            Initialize local git repo only; skip creating a GitHub remote
      --no-init-repo                         If not a git repo, exit instead of prompting to initialize one
      --project                              Write settings to .entire/settings.json even if it already exists
      --push                                 When bootstrapping a new repo, push the initial commit to the created GitHub remote (implies creating the remote; without it the repo is created but not pushed)
      --repo-name string                     GitHub repository name for the new repo (used when bootstrapping)
      --repo-owner string                    GitHub user or organization login for the new repo
      --repo-visibility string               GitHub repository visibility: public, private, or internal
      --search-skill                         Install the optional Entire search skill for selected agent(s)
      --skip-initial-commit                  Don't create the initial commit when bootstrapping a new repo
      --skip-push-sessions                   Disable automatic pushing of session logs on git push
      --telemetry                            Enable anonymous usage analytics (default true)
  -y, --yes                                  Accept all defaults without prompting (in a non-repo directory: init git, create private GitHub repo, commit, and push; then enable all agents and accept telemetry). Does not import existing agent history — see --import-history

Inherited flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

    88	// install, scaffolding, doctor and status all went on refusing the link -- with
    89	// no diagnostic, because "refused" is also what an absent grant looks like.
    90	type worktreeKey string
    91	
    92	// goosWindows is runtime.GOOS on Windows.
    93	const goosWindows = "windows"
    94	
    95	// keyFor canonicalizes a worktree root for comparison.
    96	//
    97	// Abs (which also Cleans) settles relative spellings and redundant components;
    98	// ToSlash settles the separator, which is the one that actually bit; and
    99	// Windows paths are lowered because the filesystem is case-insensitive there,
   100	// so two spellings differing only in case are the same directory and must not
   101	// key differently.
   102	//
   103	// Symlinks are deliberately NOT resolved. Both producers reach this through
   104	// git's --show-toplevel, which has already resolved them, so an EvalSymlinks
   105	// here would buy nothing and could fail on a tree being torn down.
   106	func keyFor(worktreeRoot string) worktreeKey {
   107		if worktreeRoot == "" {
   108			return ""
   109		}
   110		abs, err := filepath.Abs(worktreeRoot)
   111		if err != nil {
   112			abs = filepath.Clean(worktreeRoot)
   113		}
   114		key := filepath.ToSlash(abs)
   115		if runtime.GOOS == goosWindows {
   116			key = strings.ToLower(key)
   117		}
   118		return worktreeKey(key)
   119	}
   120	
   121	// SetVouchedSymlinkedDirs installs the set of worktree-relative agent
   122	// directories whose symlinks may be followed, replacing any previous set, and
   123	// returns the entries it refused.
   124	//
   125	// Refusal is by NAME, against the directories actually derivable from the
   126	// agents' own hook-config paths (see VouchableSymlinkedDirs). That is what keeps
   127	// the list from becoming a general "follow symlinks" switch: `.entire`,
   128	// `.git/hooks`, and anything else that is not an agent's config directory are
   129	// not spellable here at all, whoever is doing the spelling.
   130	//
   131	// The zero value vouches for nothing, so a caller that never configures a
   132	// policy gets the strict behaviour. That direction is deliberate: forgetting
   133	// this call costs a refusal the user can act on, where the opposite default
   134	// would silently follow links nobody approved.
   135	func SetVouchedSymlinkedDirs(worktreeRoot string, dirs []string) (rejected []string) {
   136		vouchable := VouchableSymlinkedDirs()
   137		accepted := make([]string, 0, len(dirs))
   138		for _, d := range dirs {
   139			clean := path.Clean(filepath.ToSlash(strings.TrimSpace(d)))
   140			clean = strings.TrimSuffix(clean, "/")
   141			if clean == "" || !slices.Contains(vouchable, clean) {
   142				rejected = append(rejected, d)
   143				continue
   144			}
   145			if !slices.Contains(accepted, clean) {
   146				accepted = append(accepted, clean)
   147			}
   148		}
   149	
   150		vouchedMu.Lock()
   151		vouchedDirs = accepted
   152		vouchedForRoot = keyFor(worktreeRoot)
   153		vouchedMu.Unlock()
   154		return rejected
   155	}
   156	
   157	// VouchedSymlinkedDirs returns the accepted set for worktreeRoot, for doctor
   158	// and status to report what is being followed rather than leaving it invisible.
   159	//
   160	// Scoped like the enforcement path, so a report can never name links that are
   161	// not in fact being followed here.
   162	func VouchedSymlinkedDirs(worktreeRoot string) []string {
   163		vouchedMu.RLock()
   164		defer vouchedMu.RUnlock()
   165		if vouchedForRoot != keyFor(worktreeRoot) {
   166			return nil
   167		}
   168		return slices.Clone(vouchedDirs)
   169	}
   170	
   171	// FollowedSymlinkedDirs is the subset of the vouched set that is a symlink on
   172	// disk right now, in worktreeRoot.
   173	//
   174	// Distinct from VouchedSymlinkedDirs, which reports the CONFIGURATION. A user
   175	// may legitimately vouch for `.claude` on a machine where it is an ordinary
"}
